articles.summary: Finance Payroll Fraud in Nigeria: Common Risks and How Businesses Can Prevent Them Oluwakemi Adesina September 7, 2026 Payroll fraud in Nigeria is usually one of the last things businesses pay attention to and that sometimes makes it a prime target. Payroll often accounts for a large share of operating costs, in service-based businesses it can run well above 40 percent, which makes it one of the biggest items on the books. Unlike procurement fraud, which usually surfaces through a missing delivery or a mismatched invoice, payroll fraud can run quietly for months because nothing about it looks out of place. This guide shows you how payroll fraud happens in Nigeria, how to spot it early, and what controls protect your business. What Is Payroll Fraud? Payroll fraud occurs when someone manipulates payroll to move money the business did not authorise. It can involve inflated payments, fake employees, or redirected salaries. Most times, it is an inside job because the person already knows the process and has access. Phishing, fake contractor payments, and vendor invoice fraud are real threats. But most payroll losses come from employees or admins with payroll access. As your business grows, informal processes that worked with 10 staff can break down at 50. Common Types of Payroll Fraud in Nigeria These fraud patterns show up in businesses of every size. Most do not need technical skill, just access and weak checks: Ghost Employees: A ghost employee is a name on the payroll with no real person behind it. It may be entirely fabricated or belong to a former employee who was never properly offboarded. If payroll removal and access revocation do not happen on the final day of employment, salaries can continue to be deposited into a bank account controlled by someone else. Falsified Overtime Claims: Overtime fraud occurs when hours never worked are submitted and approved. The risk is higher when overtime authorisation happens through informal messages or verbal sign-offs, especially for shift workers, field staff, or project teams where hours are hard to verify against output. Unauthorised Salary Increases: A salary adjustment made outside the formal review cycle without required management approval is an unauthorised increase. The risk is particularly high when the person managing employee records can also run payroll. Manipulated Bank Account Details: An administrator or employee may change a bank account number shortly before a pay run. The payroll figures still look correct, but the money is sent elsewhere. Without a process that verifies every change to bank details before payment, this can go undetected. Duplicate Salary Payments: Processing the same payroll twice or paying an employee through two channels in the same cycle creates duplicate disbursements. Manual payroll or disconnected systems increase this risk when payments are not followed by reconciliation. Payroll Data Manipulation: This includes adjusting salary figures, inflating reimbursements, or manipulating tax and pension deductions. One serious example is under-remitting statutory deductions: PAYE or pension is deducted from salaries as normal, but a lower amount is remitted to the relevant authority, and the difference is redirected. Warning Signs of Payroll Fraud Nigeria Businesses Should Watch Payroll Costs Rising Without your Headcount Growth If the salary bill increases while the headcount stays stable, investigate. A month-on-month comparison of payroll spend against active headcount can help identify unexplained growth and possible ghost employee activity. Frequent Last-Minute Payroll Changes New bank details, revised figures, or additional names submitted close to processing time are harder to scrutinise. They are not automatically fraudulent, but recurring late changes should be documented and reviewed. Bank Account Changes Without Verification Every employee bank-account update should require independent verification before a live pay run. Direct confirmation through a channel outside the payroll team’s control adds an important check. Overtime Patterns With No Operational Explanation If overtime is concentrated among a small group without a documented project, deadline, or business event to explain it, cross-check claims against attendance, output, or project records. Missing or Informal Approval Records Every salary addition, change, and disbursement should have a signed, dated, traceable approval record. WhatsApp messages, verbal conversations, or missing records create gaps in the audit trail. Duplicate Employee Records Different name variations, staff IDs, or bank accounts for the same employee require investigation. It may be an administrative error or a sign of a ghost employee scheme. Payroll Internal Controls That Close the Gaps The key is a process where more than one person reviews the numbers before money moves. Payroll compliance and fraud prevention rely on many of the same controls. Segregation of Duties The person who sets up a payroll run should not approve it or release the payment. Where teams are small, the minimum fix is to have final payment approval handled by someone outside the payroll function. Multi-Level Approval Workflows Every payroll run should require documented sign-off from more than one person. Salary changes, new hires, exits, and amendments should also require authorisation from someone who did not make the change. Approval by WhatsApp alone is not a reliable audit trail. Role-Based System Access System permissions should match job responsibilities. The administrator managing employee records should not authorise payments, the payroll processor should not freely edit salary figures, and an approved payroll run should not be editable by the approver. Verified Employee Records Every active payroll entry should correspond to a current, verified employee, with up-to-date employment records and verified bank details. Cross-checking pension deduction records with PenCom can also help verify employees and confirm that statutory obligations are being met. Payroll Audit Trails Every payroll change should be timestamped, attributed to a specific user, and retained in a log that cannot be edited after the fact. If you cannot identify who changed a bank account or salary figure and when, you are missing a basic fraud-detection mechanism. How Payroll Audits Reduce Payroll Fraud Risks A payroll audit is a scheduled, independent review of payroll data against HR records, approval logs, and statutory remittances. Its purpose is to verify that payments were authorised and deductions

articles.summary: Employee Management Employee Benefits in Nigeria: A Complete Guide for Employers Nikhil Thakur September 7, 2026 Employee benefits in Nigeria have now become a deciding factor for employees to make decisions on staying on a job. Beyond salary, candidates now ask for Health plans, Pensions plans, and other benefits the business plans to offer to make them feel comfortable. This guide covers what the law actually requires, what employees genuinely care about, and how to manage all of it. What Employee Benefits Actually Are Employee benefits are everything your employee receives beyond their base salary. The pension deduction on their payslip. The HMO card in their wallet. The annual leave days they may or may not take. The salary advance they can access when things get tight. The December bonus they quietly factor into their household budget. Together, these form the total compensation package: what the job costs your business and what it is worth to your employee. Mandatory Employee Benefits in Nigeria Pension Contributions The employer contributes at least 10% of each employee’s monthly emoluments. The employee contributes 8%. That money goes into a Retirement Savings Account (RSA) with a Pension Fund Administrator (PFA) the employee selects. National Housing Fund (NHF) The NHF requires employees earning ₦3,000 or more annually to contribute 2.5% of their basic monthly salary into the fund. Annual Leave A minimum of six days of paid annual leave after 12 months of continuous service. Maternity Leave Female employees are entitled to a minimum of 12 weeks of paid maternity leave. Some are adding paternity leave provisions even without a legal requirement, because they understand what that signal means to the people on their team. NSITF and ITF The Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) and the Industrial Training Fund (ITF) both have contribution requirements depending on your business size. Non-Mandatory Benefits: Where You Actually Compete Health Insurance A functioning HMO is one of the most valued staff benefits in Nigeria and one of the most frequently broken ones. The plan sounds strong during onboarding. Then someone’s child is sick at midnight. They spend an hour trying to reach a helpline that does not answer, only to be told by a hospital that their cover has lapsed or is not recognised. Flexible Working In Lagos, a two-hour commute each way is normal. For someone moving between the Island and Ikorodu or from Mowe to the mainland, five days in the office means four hours lost daily. If possible, a flexible working plan is a great way to reduce employee stress and help them focus. Learning and Development Employees who see growth stay. Those who feel stuck start looking for whoever offers a course, a certification, or a path. You do not need a big L&D budget. A clear policy, a few sponsored certifications, and mentorship go far. Performance Bonuses Bonuses work best when they are clear. ‘You might get something if we have a good year’ is not a motivator; it is a vague hope employees learn not to plan around. Bonuses tied to defined outcomes, communicated clearly in advance, build both performance and trust. Employee Wellness Programmes Burnout costs you in sick days, low output, and good people who are present but not engaged. Employee wellness does not need to be complex. A mental health allowance, counsellor access, or flexible leave shows you see your people as people. Recognition The quietest driver of disengagement is invisibility. Employee rewards and recognition programmes do not require a large budget. They require consistency and intentionality. A structured employee rewards and recognition approach costs less than one resignation. The absence of recognition is not neutral. It costs you. Financial Wellbeing Financial stress is the loudest background noise in most Nigerian workplaces. Employers who offer real financial wellbeing support salary advances that process in days, access to short-term credit, and payslips that clearly explain every deduction build trust no bonus structure can create. How to Structure Market-Competitive Allowances This sets your pension baseline and keeps PAYE tax exposure low. Basic Salary: Typically comprises 40% to 60% of gross pay. Housing Allowance: Accounts for 15% to 30% of the gross package to handle high urban rental costs. Transport Subsidy: Typically ranges from 10% to 15% of gross pay to offset heavy commuting expenses. 13th-Month Pay: Not a legal requirement under the Labour Act, but heavily expected as an end-of-year bonus in December. Why Employee Benefits in Nigeria Are a Retention Strategy Most business owners never calculate this: what does it cost to replace one employee? Recruitment fees or management time spent sourcing if you go direct. Multiple interview rounds. Onboarding. Three to six months before the new person is productive. The institutional knowledge, client relationships, and context that left with the person who resigned. An all-in estimate for a mid-level hire runs between three and nine months of their salary. Compare that cost to your annual benefits budget. For most Nigerian businesses, a structured employee benefits package costs less than one urgent exit. An employee who is not worried about HMO, pension, or financial emergencies is focused at work. Focused employees make better decisions, move faster, and are less likely to be looking for a new job. And then there is the employer brand effect. Your candidates might talking to your current employees before they accept any offer. The way your team describes working at your company, in conversations you will never be in, is either your best recruitment tool or your biggest liability. Benefits are always part of that conversation. Where Nigerian Businesses Sometimes Get This Wrong These are the quiet patterns that erode trust over time: Offering Benefits Nobody Uses A gym partnership sounds like a solid perk until you realise 70% of your team don’t like going to the gym. Benefits disconnected from the actual lives of your employees are not effective. Ask your team what they want before you build the package. The Benefit Exists But Nobody Knows This is common.
